extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Roman moral and legal history; general readers of 19th-century moral history
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and citation-rich discussion of Roman moral practices, legal institutions, and laws (slavery, paternal power, witnesses, gladiatorial customs, Stoicism's influence on jurisprudence) as presented in a 19th-century historical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental control after sale and enfranchisement
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was provided that if a father sold his son and if the son was afterwards enfranchised by the purchaser, he became again the slave of his father, who might sell him a second, and, if manumission again ensued, a third time. It was only on the third sale that he passed for ever out of the parental control.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of the Roman legal rule governing the effect of sale and subsequent manumission on patria potestas; presented as a formal legal provision (cited to Dion. Halicarn. ii. 4 in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of paternal power by marriage (Numa's law)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A more merciful law, attributed to Numa, provided that when the son married (if that marriage was with the consent of the father), the father lost the power of selling him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes an historical legal exception limiting the father's right to sell his son once the son married with paternal consent; presented as a comparatively humane innovation in the law of patria potestas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of paternal authority (rights over life and adultery)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A Roman had originally not only absolute authority over the life of his son, but also the right of killing any one whom he found committing adultery with his wife.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records the extreme scope of early Roman paterfamilias powers (including capital action for adultery) and contextualizes later legal/moral moderation (e.g., Marcian praising Hadrian’s restraint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for calling slaves as witnesses and for using torture
rubrics_metrics.description: “Slaves were only to be called as witnesses in cases of incest, adultery, murder, and high treason, and where it was impossible to establish the crime without their evidence. Hadrian considered that the reality of the crime must have already acquired a strong probability, and the jurisconsult Paul laid down that at least two free witnesses should be heard before slaves were submitted to torture, and that the offer of an accused person to have his slaves tortured that they might attest his innocence should not be accepted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies procedural safeguards and narrow substantive circumstances under which slave testimony (and torture) could be used in Roman practice; cites Hadrian and the jurisconsult Paul as authorities limiting reliance on slave evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition rights of public/state slaves
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was customary to allow the public or State slaves to dispose of half their goods by will.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes an established legal/customary allowance giving certain testamentary rights to public/state slaves; presented as a particular rule about property rights of slaves under Roman practice (cited to Plin. Epist. viii. 16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law against atrocious cruelty to slaves (imperial sanction)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hadrian exiled a Roman lady for five years for treating her slaves with atrocious cruelty. (Digest lib. i. tit. 6, § 2.)”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that imperial law/policy could punish severe cruelty to slaves; the example of Hadrian is given to show concrete sanction and legal redress against extreme mistreatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of jurisprudence and natural law (Ulpian, Paul, Gaius)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ulpian defined jurisprudence as “divinarum atque humanarum rerum notitia, justi atque injusti scientia.” Paul: “Id quod semper æquum ad bonum est jus dicitur ut est jus naturale.” Gaius: formulations on the distinctive Roman patria potestas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents classical juristic definitions used as foundational concepts in Roman legal thought (Ulpian, Paul, Gaius); these definitions function as normative conceptions of law and justice in the Roman tradition as discussed in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rival schools of Roman jurisprudent interpretation (Labeo vs Capito)
rubrics_metrics.description: “There were two rival schools, that of Labeo and that of Capito. The first was remarkable for its strict adherence to the letter of the law—the second for the latitude of interpretation it admitted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes competing hermeneutic/interpretive standards among Roman jurists: literal, letter-bound interpretation (Labeo) versus broader, more flexible interpretation (Capito); useful as a criterion for understanding juridical reasoning and legal development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate decree abolishing regular human sacrifices (dating and legal change)
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Pliny, “regular human sacrifices were only abolished in Rome by a decree of the senate, B.C. 97,” though some instances occurred later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records a formal senatorial legal prohibition on an entrenched religious/legal practice (human sacrifice), noting the formal legal abolition date and the persistence of isolated instances thereafter (used as evidence of legal-cultural change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative attempts and violations regulating elite conduct (e.g., patricians in gladiatorial combats)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Laws prohibiting patricians from fighting were several times made and violated.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates that statutes existed to regulate elite behaviour (here, forbidding patrician participation in gladiatorial fighting) but were not always enforced—serves as a standard versus practice contrast in Roman legal/social norms.
